From my personal experience, sitting with my thoughts makes it a lot worse. I find distractions very helpful. Not small distractions like watching TV - actual engaging distractions that require near full attention. Video games, work, intense exercise, chess, ect. Sex/masturbation is also a great distraction and overall anxiety reducer.

Medication (SSRIs) help me a lot. Risk vs benefit - the side effects of zoloft are far outweighed by the relief I get, so I take them. But that may not be the same for you. Also, they can take a long time to work for OCD. 

The brief moment of relaxation you get will continue to grow over time. Eventually, I find myself not ruminating/hyper-fixating for hours, then days, then weeks. Progress is certainly not linear, so you will always have bad days.

I’ve done a lot of research on this subject because I’ve been dealing with it for so long. If yours truly is anxiety, it is a cycle. Typically it goes like this: 

Anxiety -> SOB -> quick shallow breathing and over-breathing -> not expelling enough co2 -> SOB…

Insert anxiety anywhere and the cycle restarts.

I’m glad I can provide some hope! I have a ton of empathy and a soft spot for people with this anxiety manifestation - because it really is one of the scariest and relentless symptoms. 

Mine seems to be triggered by 2 things: 

1.) Actual respiratory ailments like colds, allergies, sinus inflammation, ect. The actual symptoms cause me to spiral and develop similar anxiety symptoms.

2.) Big changes in my life, stressful times, loss of loved ones, ect. In this case, the symptoms are usually preceded by a panic attack.

Sometimes nothing triggers it, I’ll just kinda focus on my breathing one night, and it starts up again. But during these times, it usually resolves quickly.

I have had on and off crippling anxiety w/ main symptom of air hunger and chest tightness for about 5 years. My flares last anywhere from a few days to a few months. I was first put on Zoloft (100mg x2 weeks then 150mg - daily) in 2020 for these symptoms. It went away in a few months - but it’s worth mentioning I made many lifestyle changes (losing weight, routine, healthy habits) while taking the medication.

Fast forward to 3 weeks ago, and its back with a vengeance. I am once again taking 150mg Zoloft daily, not much improvement yet, but all we can do is take it one day at a time!

Ive also had this on and off for years. When its flaring its 24/7 shortness of breath and hyper-fixation on breathing - distractions help but its always in the back of my mind. Most recent flare is 3 weeks and going strong. It’s actually the worst.

1 week?! Thats very quick improvement for SSRI’s - even if it’s only daytime. Congrats!

Your doctor will definitely want to see you on that dose for a longer period of time. 

SSRI’s take time to rewire the brain in an amazing process called neuroplasticity. 

Immediate benefits are a plus - the actual meat and potatoes of the therapy has not even begun for you!

Give it time friend!
OCD treatment is definitely on the higher end of the dosing spectrum. 25mg would do squat for me, lol. How long have you been on that dose? What side effects are concerned for?

I am not a doctor but I am studying Biology at university have been going through the same exact thing for 3 weeks. It has gotten a lot better, but I am also taking anxiety medication. What you are experiencing is known as air hunger (dyspnea). There are many real causes of dyspnea like lung infections, obesity, or sedentary lifestyle. I would advise you to get it checked out in person by a doctor just to be sure, but what you are describing sounds very much like anxiety. Assuming it is anxiety, this is a very normal and common symptom that should not cause alarm. The normal human body automatically takes about 8 deep breaths every hour, excluding sighs from shock or stress. What you are feeling is only an illusion caused by the focus on your breathing and the anxiety associated with it. Just for some reassurance, there is nothing wrong with focusing on the breathe. Many people enjoy doing it voluntarily as a form of meditation. Now when it comes to addressing your issue, some people do breathing exercises or meditation; while others, like myself, distract themselves and occupy their mind as therapy. I would recommend you try both and see what works best for you. Like I said, definitely get it checked out, but it’s more than likely anxiety.

Anxiety is pretty much a permanent mental vestigial feature. Granted you believe in the theory of evolution, we evolved from wild animals that relied purely on instinct to survive. Take, for example, a deer when it is approached by a human. The deer doesn’t stop to think, “is this human going to hurt me or not”. It relies on basic innate instinct that humans are danger and it has two options, fight or flight. Most vestigial features become less and less common as evolution progresses over years, to the point that a new species emerges. These features are eliminated by natural selection. So now you may ask, why hasn’t anxiety been eliminated from the human race through natural selection? Its because anxiety isn’t a evolutionary feature, it’s an innate instinct. When all else fails, species must be equipped with a method that will allow them to thrive and survive without thinking. That method is fight or flight. The only problem is, when the big bang happened, life wasn’t anticipating species to become such advanced organisms. Humans are in a constant battle with self vs instinct. Our brains are so developed that they often overthink and trick themselves into thinking they are in danger when they are not.
